notes: West leads the ♠10 against 6NT. South has only 8 top tricks (3 spades, 3 hearts, and 2 clubs). The ♦K can knock out the ♦A and establish the ♦Q as trick 9. The other 3 tricks can be taken in clubs if the ♣Q can be picked up.

There are two alternatives to consider in playing the club suit. South can cash the ♣A and ♣K hoping clubs are 2-2 as above. This play will also work when either West or East has a singleton ♣Q and when East has all 4 clubs. In the latter case, West will show out on the first top club and South can finesse East out of his known ♣Q by leading through him twice from the North hand.

The alternative play is to finesse East for the ♣Q after cashing one top honour. This line of play gains over the first one when East has 3 clubs to the Queen, but loses to West's Queen doubleton of clubs.
The mathematics of all of these possibilities favours cashing the top honours. That is, cashing the ♣A and ♣K is slightly more likely to work than taking the second round finesse.

A famous bridge saying can be used to help you remember this play. "8 ever, 9 never" means that if North and South have 8 cards in a suit missing only the Queen, it is correct to finesse for the Queen. With 9 cards between the 2 hands, as above, it is correct to play for the drop.

The order in which the ♠A and ♠K are cashed is critical. If West has all 4 spades, nothing can be done. Even if the ♠A is cashed first, West can cover South's continuation of the ♠J or ♠10 with his ♠Q, making his ♠9 and ♠8 into a sure trick.

If East has all 4 spades, South can pick up the suit by cashing the ♠K first. He can subsequently finesse twice against East's ♠Q. This play is marked as West's spade void will show up when the ♠K is cashed. South can get to dummy in hearts to take a second finesse against East's ♠Q. Cashing the ♠K first is superior to cashing the ♠A as the former play picks up all 4 spades in East's hand.
If both defenders follow to the ♠K, South should play his ♠A on the second round ("9 never".

notes: West leads the ♦A against 4♥. West wins the first trick and continues diamonds. South has a critical decision to make. Should South play the ♦K or finesse at trick 2?

The easiest way to solve this problem is to think about what could go wrong with each play. If the ♦K is played and East ruffs, the contract will fail. East will return a spade and South will have no way of avoiding losing a trick in both spades and diamonds.

If the diamond finesse is taken at trick 2, nothing can go wrong. East may win the ♦Q and return a spade. North's diamond suit is now established to provide discards for South's spade and club losers once trump is drawn.
If East started with a singleton diamond, he will ruff at trick 2. Dummy's diamonds will again be established to take care of South's spade and club losers.

South does better by cashing the ♥A and leading hearts towards North's honours, twice if necessary. The contract will make anytime West has the ♥K or when East has a singleton ♥K or when East has 3 hearts to the ♥K.

South has two alternatives. First, he can lead the ♣Q, playing East to have a singleton ♣J. Second, he can cash the ♣A playing either defender to have a singleton ♣K. There are two ways to play the club suit to guarantee only 1 loser, regardless of how that suit divides. First, South can start by leading a small club out of his hand. If West follows with the ♣5, a low club is played from dummy. If West discards on South's club lead, the ♣A is played from North. A club is led towards South's ♣Q, holding East to 1 club trick.

Alternatively, South can cross to dummy in spades and play a club towards his ♣Q. If East plays any club, South has an easy time. If East discards, South can play either a low club or the ♣Q and later finesse against West's other club honour.

If West returns a trump after winning the ♦Q, South should decline the finesse, rising with North's ♠A. South can afford to lose a trick to the ♠K. However, he cannot afford to lose a trick to East before he discards a club on North's ♦J. If East has the ♠K and West the ♣A, finessing in spades would be fatal.
South should play the ♦J from dummy and take his club discard before continuing spades. South will lose just 2 more tricks, the ♠K and the ♣A.
